Autoresearch

Autoresearch makes Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse keep improving your code on its own.

It is based on Karpathy's autoresearch. A constraint, a mechanical metric, and autonomous iteration together produce gains that compound.

"Set the GOAL → The agent runs the LOOP → You wake up to results"

AGI isn't required. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that keeps running.

Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse are supported for the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush: metric loops get out of plateaus using the method from Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447). The loop forks at 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep. It starts fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each one briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches choose their own ideas, which adds randomness. Each branch in the other half gets a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it tries FORK before giving up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee is a read-only tool that collects package, extension, and developer-tool metadata from macOS and Linux developer machines.

It is built for one supply-chain response question. When an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines currently show a match in their on-disk metadata?

An SBOM tells you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs something else: the untidy local state spread across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and the developer-tool configs Bumblebee supports.

Bumblebee reads that scattered on-disk state and writes it out as structured NDJSON component records. Give it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches. Responders who already know what they are looking for get a fast exposure check that changes nothing on the machine.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks in a range of domains. It measures how much better a model handles complex real-world tasks when it has specialized Skills available.

In production, many Skills are often installed at once. To test performance under those conditions, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In our version, every task runs in a shared environment with all 195 specialized Skills installed, and all other experimental conditions stay the same.
